articles.title: How to Choose Personalised Workwear for Your Team
articles.deck: A practical guide to custom workwear, branded workwear and company clothing with a logo.
articles.meta: Choose personalised workwear for your team by comparing garments, fabrics, logo methods, sizing and working conditions.
articles.alt: Team wearing coordinated personalised workwear with embroidered company logos
sections: Start with the job rather than the garment

The best personalised workwear starts with the work being done. A garment that performs well at reception may be unsuitable for a warehouse, building site or commercial kitchen. Before selecting products, list where employees work, how much they move, whether they face customers and how often the clothing will be washed.

This approach prevents a common mistake: choosing one item because it looks good online and then trying to make it serve every role. Custom workwear should form a small coordinated system. Everyday tops, warm layers, outerwear and role-specific garments can share the same colours and logo positions without being identical.
Choose fabric by use and care

Cotton feels familiar and comfortable, making it a strong option for many T shirts and polo shirts. Polyester can dry quickly and suit active roles. Polycotton blends are widely used for branded workwear because they balance comfort, durability and easier care. Fabric weight matters, but it should never be treated as the only measure of quality.

Check the care label against the real laundry routine. If garments will be washed frequently, the product and decoration method must support that routine. A uniform that looks excellent on delivery but is difficult to maintain will cost more through early replacement.
Build a simple uniform range

Start with one main top, one mid layer and one outer layer where needed. A trade team may use printed workwear T shirts, embroidered workwear polos, hoodies and softshell jackets. A customer-facing team may prefer polo shirts, knitwear and smart jackets. Limiting the number of approved products makes repeat ordering easier and keeps the team consistent.

Use one value range, one balanced range and one premium range when comparing products. The cheapest option is not always the lowest-cost choice if it loses shape, feels uncomfortable or needs replacing sooner.
Match the logo method to the product

Embroidery gives company clothing with a logo a textured, professional finish and works particularly well on polos, sweatshirts, fleeces, caps and jackets. DTF and DTG can reproduce detailed colour artwork. Screen printing is strong for suitable designs at higher quantities. The correct method depends on the garment, artwork, position and order size.

Large areas should not automatically be embroidered. Dense stitching can feel heavy and may distort lighter fabrics. A compact chest logo can be embroidered while a large back design is printed, giving one uniform the right finish in both positions.
Approve one complete specification

Confirm the product code, colour, sizes, quantities, logo version, position, approximate size and customisation method before production. Check names, phone numbers and website addresses carefully. Save this approved specification so future orders reproduce the same branded workwear instead of starting again.
Branded UK supplies and customises workwear from its Surbiton workshop. Standard production is normally 7 to 10 working days after artwork approval and payment, subject to stock and capacity.

articles.title: Workwear Embroidery and Logo Embroidery Explained
articles.deck: What happens between uploading a logo and receiving finished embroidered workwear.
articles.meta: Learn how workwear embroidery is produced, why logos need digitising and which garments and designs suit embroidered branding.
articles.alt: Industrial embroidery machine stitching a company logo onto workwear
sections: What workwear embroidery actually involves

Workwear embroidery uses coloured thread to build a logo directly into the garment. The result has texture, depth and a professional appearance that suits uniforms worn repeatedly. Logo embroidery is commonly used on polo shirts, sweatshirts, fleeces, jackets, caps, aprons and many other stable fabrics.

The machine cannot sew directly from a JPEG or standard logo file. The design must first be converted into stitch instructions. This process is called digitising and controls stitch type, direction, density, underlay and sewing order.
Why digitising matters

A good embroidery file is designed around the fabric and the final size. The same artwork may require different settings for a polo shirt and a structured cap. Fine details can close up, small gaps can disappear and thin lettering may become difficult to read if the file is prepared without considering thread and fabric movement.

Digitising is not a visual filter. It is production engineering. A skilled operator decides where stitches begin and end, which areas need support and how the design should run efficiently without losing its identity.
Artwork that embroiders well

Bold shapes, clear lettering and compact logos normally produce reliable embroidered workwear. Very small text, photographic shading, distressed textures and fine gradients may need simplification. This is not a reduction in quality; it is an adjustment from flat artwork to a physical thread construction.

Send the original vector artwork where possible. If it is unavailable, provide the largest clean image you have. Avoid screenshots and logos copied from a website because they often contain blurred edges and incorrect colours.
Garments and positions

Left chest logo embroidery is the standard choice for professional uniforms. Right chest can carry a name, role or secondary mark. Sleeves work well for compact flags or accreditations. Caps require specific consideration because seams, crown shape and frames affect the sewing area.

Large dense back logos are possible in some cases but are often better printed. They can become heavy, stiff and expensive in thread. The garment and position should be assessed before the method is confirmed.
Checking the finished result

Approval should cover logo version, colours, position and size. Screen colours are not identical to physical thread, so brand references should be supplied when colour accuracy matters. Production checks should include spelling, alignment, loose threads, fabric stability and overall appearance.
Branded UK operates an eight-head Barudan embroidery machine in Surbiton, allowing repeat production across team orders while each garment is checked before finishing.

articles.title: Personalised Polo Shirts Buying Guide
articles.deck: How to compare personalised, embroidered and printed polo shirts for work.
articles.meta: Compare personalised polo shirts by fabric, fit, weight, wash care and logo method before ordering embroidered or printed polos.
articles.alt: Embroidered personalised polo shirts arranged in coordinated company colours
sections: Why polo shirts work across many industries

Polo shirts sit between T shirts and formal shirts, making them suitable for trades, offices, hospitality, events and sports staff. They look organised without restricting movement and can be combined with sweatshirts, fleeces or jackets to create complete staff uniforms.

The correct product depends on how it will be worn. A cotton polo may suit front-of-house use, while a polyester performance polo can be better for active work. A polycotton polo is a dependable middle option for many everyday uniforms.
Cotton polycotton and performance fabrics

Cotton offers softness and a familiar feel but can absorb moisture and take longer to dry. Polycotton blends balance comfort with easier care and durability. Polyester performance polos are designed for quicker drying and can suit warm or active environments.
Do not choose by fibre alone. Collar construction, placket, stitching, side vents, fit and opacity affect how personalised polo shirts look after repeated wear.
Embroidered polo shirts

Embroidered polo shirts are the most common choice for professional company uniforms. A compact left chest logo is visible during customer interaction and gives the garment a premium finish. Names or roles can be added on the opposite chest when required.
Thin lettering and intricate artwork should be reviewed at the intended size. A logo that looks clear on a large monitor may need small changes to remain readable in thread.
Printed polo shirts

Printed polo shirts work well when the design contains gradients, several colours or a larger back graphic. DTF can reproduce detailed logos at smaller quantities, while screen printing can be efficient for suitable volume orders. The fabric must be checked before heat or ink is applied.
A useful combination is an embroidered chest logo with a printed back design. This keeps the front refined while making the company visible from a distance.
Fit sizing and repeat orders

Use the size guide for the exact product rather than relying on the size employees usually buy. Where possible, offer equivalent fits for different body shapes while keeping colour and branding consistent. For larger teams, a sample fitting can prevent avoidable exchanges.
Record the product code, garment colour, logo file, thread or print colours, position and size. This turns the first order into a reliable specification for replacements and new starters.

articles.title: Custom T Shirts and T Shirt Printing Guide
articles.deck: Choose the right garment and printing method for custom clothing, events, teams and businesses.
articles.meta: Plan custom T shirts by comparing fabric, weight, fit, DTF, DTG and screen printing for business, event and team orders.
articles.alt: Custom T shirts showing DTF DTG and screen printed company designs
sections: Begin with how the T shirt will be used

Custom T shirts can serve as daily staff clothing, event uniforms, promotional products, merchandise or teamwear. The use determines the correct garment. A short event may prioritise budget and colour availability, while daily personalised clothing needs comfort, wash performance and dependable repeat stock.
Choose the garment before finalising the print method. Fibre content, fabric colour and surface affect how ink or transfers appear.
Light medium and heavyweight T shirts

Lightweight T shirts feel cooler and can suit events or warm conditions. Medium weights are versatile for staff uniforms and promotions. Heavyweight styles create a more substantial, retail-inspired shape and can support premium custom clothing.
Weight alone does not guarantee quality. Fit, knitting, collar construction, side seams, colourfastness and shrinkage guidance should also be checked.
DTF and DTG printing

DTF printing places a detailed transfer onto the garment and works across many suitable fabrics. It handles multiple colours and fine artwork without preparing a separate screen for every colour. It is useful for smaller batches, names and designs that change between orders.

DTG printing applies ink directly to a compatible garment. It is particularly effective for detailed artwork on suitable cotton-rich T shirts and can produce a softer feel than a large solid transfer. Garment composition and pretreatment affect the result.
Screen printing for volume

Screen printing is a strong choice for clear designs at larger quantities. Each colour normally requires preparation, so the setup becomes more economical as the order quantity increases. Branded UK normally applies a minimum of 25 items for screen printed orders.
The design may need colour separation or simplification. Once prepared correctly, screen printing produces consistent repeated results across a team or event order.
Prepare the artwork and quantities

Supply vector artwork for logos and flat graphics whenever possible. Use high-resolution original files for photographic designs. Confirm the front, back and sleeve positions separately and state whether the same design appears on every garment.

The normal Branded UK minimum is eight items, subject to product and method. Screen printing and specific product types can have higher minimums. Confirm sizes and quantities on one approved sheet before production.

articles.title: DTF Printing vs DTG Printing vs Screen Printing
articles.deck: A clear comparison of three garment printing methods and when each one works best.
articles.meta: Compare DTF printing, DTG printing and screen printing by garment, design, quantity, finish and setup before placing an order.
articles.alt: DTF DTG and screen printing samples compared on custom garments
sections: DTF printing

Direct to film printing produces the artwork on a film before it is applied to the garment with heat and pressure. DTF printing can reproduce detailed, multi-colour logos and works on many compatible fabrics. It is often suitable for printed workwear, smaller orders, changing names and designs with gradients.
The print sits on the fabric, so large solid areas can feel different from the garment around them. Correct temperature, pressure, transfer quality and garment compatibility are essential.
DTG printing

Direct to garment printing applies ink directly to the garment. DTG printing is strong for detailed, full-colour images on suitable cotton-rich products. The ink interacts with the fabric, which can create a softer result than a solid transfer.

It is not the automatic choice for every workwear fabric. Polyester blends, technical treatments and some colours may require another process. The garment should be confirmed before the design is prepared around DTG.
Screen printing

Screen printing uses a prepared screen to apply each colour. It is efficient for suitable designs at volume and is widely used for staff T shirts, event clothing and repeated promotional orders. Bold artwork with a controlled number of colours is an ideal starting point.
Because each colour requires setup, screen printing is normally less economical for very small quantities. The Branded UK minimum is generally 25 items for this method.
Which method should you choose

Choose DTF for detailed colour, flexible garment use and smaller runs. Choose DTG for detailed artwork on compatible cotton-rich garments where a direct print is appropriate. Choose screen printing for repeated designs at quantities that justify setup.
These are starting points rather than fixed rules. Artwork size, fabric, product colour, order volume and the expected finish must be considered together.
Combining methods

One order can use more than one method. A polo or jacket may carry a small embroidered chest logo while T shirts use screen printing and hi vis garments use DTF on the back. Consistent branding does not require an identical process on every product.
Send the full garment list and artwork together. This allows the production team to choose the correct process for every position while keeping colour and scale controlled.

articles.title: How to Plan Corporate Uniforms and Staff Uniforms
articles.deck: Create branded uniforms that look consistent, fit different roles and remain easy to reorder.
articles.meta: Plan corporate uniforms and staff uniforms by role, garment, colour, logo placement, allocation and repeat ordering.
articles.alt: Office and operations team wearing coordinated corporate uniforms
sections: Define roles before choosing products

Corporate uniforms should reflect what employees actually do. Reception, office, warehouse, delivery and management teams may need different garments, but they can still share colours and branding. Start by grouping roles with similar working conditions rather than ordering one product for everyone.
This makes staff uniforms more comfortable and improves the likelihood that employees will wear them correctly.
Build a controlled product range
Choose a core top, warm layer and outer layer for each role. Keep the range tight enough to maintain consistency. Too many similar options make approvals, stock and repeat orders harder to manage.
Branded uniforms can include different fits without losing their identity. Use equivalent colours and logo placement across men’s, women’s and unisex garments where the range supports them.
Set colour and logo rules
Record approved garment colours, logo versions, thread or print colours, positions and sizes. If the company has light and dark logo variations, specify which one belongs on each garment colour.
A chest logo normally provides sufficient recognition for customer-facing roles. Larger back designs can support delivery, event or service teams where distance visibility matters.
Calculate employee allocations

The number of garments depends on working days, laundry frequency, role and season. Many full-time employees require several everyday tops but fewer mid layers and jackets. Part-time and occasional staff need a different allocation.
Keep a controlled reserve for common sizes and new starters. Large speculative stock ties up cash and can become unusable if the product or branding changes.
Create a repeat-order system

Store the approved product codes, colours, sizes, artwork and personalisation data in one place. Managers should reorder from this range instead of choosing new products each time. This protects brand consistency and shortens the approval process.
Review replacement rates and staff feedback after the first season. Real usage data is more useful than a fixed uniform rule borrowed from another company.

articles.title: Hospitality Uniforms for Cafés Restaurants and Hotels
articles.deck: Plan practical hospitality uniforms that stay comfortable through service and support the customer experience.
articles.meta: Choose hospitality uniforms for cafés, restaurants, bars and hotels by comparing roles, fabrics, fits, aprons and logo methods.
articles.alt: Hospitality team wearing coordinated embroidered uniforms and aprons
sections: Plan by role and environment

Front of house, bar, kitchen, housekeeping, delivery and management teams work differently. Hospitality uniforms should recognise those differences while maintaining one visual identity. A shirt may suit reception, while personalised polo shirts or T shirts can work better in active casual service.
Outdoor areas and deliveries may also require a branded layer that is not used inside.
Choose fabrics for heat movement and washing

Hospitality garments experience heat, movement, spills and frequent laundering. Check breathability, drying time, opacity, stain visibility and care instructions. The fabric should support the shift rather than only look good in a photograph.
Test the actual colour. Black can look smart but may show flour and lint. Light colours can create a clean appearance but need an appropriate laundry and replacement plan.
Use aprons as part of the uniform

Bib, waist and cross-back aprons create a strong branding area and help distinguish roles. Compare pockets, strap adjustment, fabric weight and wash care. Position the logo where it remains visible when the apron is tied and the pockets are used.
Embroidery gives stable apron fabrics a premium finish. Printing can suit larger or more detailed artwork.
Offer suitable fits

One nominally unisex garment will not suit every team member. Where possible, offer equivalent fits while keeping colours and branding consistent. Use product-specific size guides and sample fitting for larger staff groups.
Comfort matters commercially. Staff who feel restricted or overheated are less likely to wear the uniform as intended.
Keep repeat orders controlled

Hospitality teams can change throughout the year. Record product codes, colours, logo settings and employee sizes so new starters receive the correct garments quickly. A controlled range prevents gradual changes that make the team look inconsistent.
Branded UK can combine embroidered workwear, printed garments and aprons into one repeatable hospitality uniform package.

articles.title: Construction Workwear and Custom Hi Vis Workwear Guide
articles.deck: Build a practical layered uniform for trades, contractors and site teams.
articles.meta: Plan construction workwear and custom hi vis workwear with suitable layers, branding positions, durability and repeat ordering.
articles.alt: Construction team wearing branded workwear and custom hi vis garments
sections: Build the uniform in layers

Construction workwear must adapt to physical work, changing weather, early starts and customer contact. Begin with T shirts or polos, add sweatshirts, hoodies or fleeces, then select softshells, waterproofs or insulated jackets where required.
Layering gives employees practical choices without losing a coordinated company appearance.
Choose products around the task

Fabric strength, pockets, knee protection, stretch, weather resistance and fit matter more than appearance alone. Site workers, supervisors, drivers and customer-facing trades may need different products.
Keep the core colours and logo positions consistent so the range still reads as one company uniform.
Custom hi vis workwear

A bright garment is not automatically certified hi vis. Select the product for the relevant site requirement and keep reflective tape unobstructed. Branding must be positioned only within suitable areas and should never be presented as proof of compliance.
Large back printing can improve company recognition at distance. A chest logo supports identification during customer contact. Product documentation should be checked before decoration.
Embroidery and print on outerwear

Polos, sweatshirts, fleeces and many softshells suit embroidery. Embroidered jackets require checks around lining access, waterproof construction and insulation. Needle penetration may be inappropriate for some technical products.
DTF or screen printing can suit large back designs and selected hi vis garments. Heat compatibility must be confirmed before production.
Plan replacements

Trade clothing experiences heavy wear and staining. Record the issue date, product, size and employee allocation. Use replacement data to plan future orders instead of buying a large unmeasured reserve.
A repeatable custom workwear package keeps new starters and replacement orders consistent across the year.

articles.title: Healthcare Uniforms Buying Guide
articles.deck: Choose healthcare uniforms that support movement, frequent washing and clear team identification.
articles.meta: Choose healthcare uniforms by comparing tunics, polos, scrubs, fabric, fit, laundering, role colours and logo customisation.
articles.alt: Healthcare staff wearing coordinated personalised uniforms
sections: Start with the care environment

Healthcare uniforms vary between clinics, dental practices, care homes, therapy businesses, reception teams and community staff. Begin with movement, contact, temperature and laundering requirements before selecting a style.
A reception polo and a clinical tunic may share the same colour and logo without serving the same function.
Check fabric and laundering

Confirm the wash instructions for the specific garment and compare them with the organisation’s laundry process. Frequent washing, drying and stain treatment can affect colour, fit and decoration. Do not assume every garment can be washed at the same temperature.
Breathability, stretch, pocket placement and opacity should be evaluated during movement.
Use colour to identify roles

Colour can help distinguish teams or responsibilities, but the system should remain simple. Too many colours create ordering problems and make replacement difficult. Record the approved colour for every role and avoid substituting a visually similar shade without approval.
The logo should contrast clearly and remain consistent across the colour range.
Choose suitable customisation

Compact embroidery can give healthcare uniforms a durable professional finish. Fine text and very lightweight fabrics need review. DTF printing may suit detailed logos on compatible garments, while names or roles can be added where the organisation requires them.
Personal information and role titles must be checked carefully before production.
Maintain an approved range
Keep a controlled list of tunics, polos, scrubs, fleeces or outer layers used by each role. Store sizes and allocations securely and update them when staff change.
This makes personalised clothing easier to reorder and avoids mismatched colours or logo positions across the team.

articles.title: Sports Team Clothing and Clubwear Guide
articles.deck: Plan playing kit, staff clothing, travel wear and supporter garments as one coordinated range.
articles.meta: Plan sports team clothing for players, coaches, staff and supporters with suitable products, logo positions and sponsor branding.
articles.alt: Sports team wearing coordinated custom club clothing
sections: Separate performance kit from club clothing

Playing garments, warm-up layers, travel wear, coach clothing and supporter merchandise serve different purposes. Sports team clothing works best when these groups are planned together but not forced into one fabric or fit.
Use shared colours, club marks and sponsor rules to keep the range connected.
Choose products by activity

Performance T shirts and polos can support training and coaching. Personalised hoodies, sweatshirts and jackets provide warm layers before and after activity. Custom T shirts can serve events, fundraising and supporters.
Check mobility, drying time, fit and layering. A product that works for travel may not perform during training.
Control crests names and numbers

Maintain one approved crest and sponsor artwork pack. Confirm positions, sizes and colours for each garment type. Names and numbers should be supplied on one final data sheet to reduce spelling and duplication errors.
Embroidery can suit crests on polos, caps, hoodies and embroidered jackets. Printing is normally more practical for large numbers, names and back graphics.
Plan size and quantity

Collect assigned player and staff sizes against the exact product guide. Merchandise stock requires a different approach based on previous sales, audience and event size. Do not apply the player size mix to supporter products without evidence.
Keep a small controlled reserve for new players and replacements where the club’s turnover justifies it.
Make reordering simple

Record every approved garment, colour and decoration setting. A club range should remain easy to reproduce during the season. Changing suppliers or near-matching colours without review can create visible inconsistency.
Branded UK can produce coordinated custom clothing for players, coaches, staff and club events from one approved specification.

articles.title: Personalised Hoodies Sweatshirts and Embroidered Jackets
articles.deck: Compare warm workwear layers and choose the correct logo method for each product.
articles.meta: Compare personalised hoodies, embroidered hoodies, custom sweatshirts and embroidered jackets for work, teams and events.
articles.alt: Personalised hoodies custom sweatshirts and embroidered jackets displayed together
sections: Choose the layer by working condition

Hoodies, sweatshirts and jackets solve different problems. Custom sweatshirts create a clean crew-neck layer for uniforms. Personalised hoodies add warmth and a more casual appearance. Jackets provide weather protection or insulation. Choose by environment and role rather than treating every warm garment as interchangeable.
A coordinated range can use all three while maintaining the same colours and chest logo.
Pullover and zipped hoodies

Pullover hoodies provide an uninterrupted front and work well for teams, trades and events. Zipped hoodies are easier to remove and can support changing indoor temperatures. Pockets, drawcords, zips and seams affect the available branding area.
Embroidered hoodies work well with compact logos. Large back artwork is normally better printed.
Crew-neck sweatshirts

Custom sweatshirts offer warmth without a hood and can look more uniform beneath jackets. Check cuff recovery, waistband, fabric weight, fit and wash care. Polycotton blends are common for everyday workwear, while premium cotton-rich styles can create a softer retail feel.
Chest embroidery is a dependable choice. DTF or screen printing can support larger graphics.
Embroidered jackets

Softshells, fleeces, padded jackets and waterproofs behave differently during embroidery. Lining, insulation, coatings, panels and access points must be assessed. Embroidered jackets should never be approved solely from a flat product image.
Some technical garments require a print method or a different branding position to protect performance and appearance.
Create a consistent warm layer range

Limit the approved colours and use one logo specification wherever the garment construction allows. Record any necessary position changes for pockets, panels or zips. Staff should be able to combine layers without the branding appearing inconsistent.
Order enough mid layers for the working pattern, but avoid excessive stock. Review actual use after the colder season before repeating the quantity.
